pages.title: Install and activate Blackbird
pages.description: Install Blackbird, choose packages, and finish activation.
pages.body:
## Before you start
Use the Windows installer offered on the [Blackbird product page](/en/products/blackbird/). This guide describes the upcoming package-enabled version; an older installed version may have different package controls. Blackbird does not install your game engine, Android tools, or storefront upload utilities for you. Add those only when a task needs them.

## Install
1. Download the EXE installer for ordinary interactive setup, or use the MSI if your deployment process requires it.
2. Run the installer and follow its location and package-selection screens. Choose the bundles for the tools you use. System Information is required and remains available for the first-run tutorial.
3. Open Blackbird. Let initial package setup finish before running work.
4. Follow the activation or trial options shown by your build. Use your own issued license or redemption information; do not share it in screenshots or support posts.
5. Run [System Information](../first-action/) to confirm the basic Action workflow works.

Packages can be changed later under **Settings > Packages**. You do not need an engine project or a connected device for the first Action.

## If setup does not finish
Read the reported error before rerunning setup. A folder-access failure can mean the destination is not writable or another program is using it. Close the identified program or choose a writable location. Do not delete your library or configuration to retry an update.

If activation fails, confirm you are using the intended license information and the instructions in the activation screen. Include the error text when contacting support, but omit the license itself. Installation and license state are not a substitute for the external tools required by individual Actions.
pages.media: Screenshot: the installer bundle-selection screen with Utilities and one engine selected; visibly retain required System Information. Second screenshot: the activation choices with all license values blank. Caption what users can change later; do not depict private licensing tools.

pages.title: Run your first Action
pages.description: Check Blackbird with System Information before configuring tools.
pages.body:
## Run System Information
1. Open **Actions** in the sidebar.
2. Select **Clear filters** if a filter is active.
3. Search for **System Information**.
4. Select **Run** on its card or row.
5. Read the completion window, then close it.

This Action requires neither an active project nor an external device. It reports your operating system, architecture, PowerShell, Blackbird runtime, and ADB availability. **ADB: Not found** does not mean this test failed. You only need ADB for Android work.

## What you just used
An **Action** is a single task. **Run** starts that task after any required configuration or confirmation. **Queue** saves it into the working queue for later. Results appear in a completion window; detailed messages remain in **Output** and past runs in **History**.

For this Action, the expected result is a System Information window reporting that Blackbird is ready. If it is missing from search, clear filters and check **Settings > Packages**. If the run fails, use the error and log to investigate rather than installing unrelated engines or device software.

## Next steps
Add a project if your next task needs one. Otherwise, continue browsing Actions. You can revisit the in-app tutorials from **Settings > General > Getting Started**; closing a tutorial does not prevent ordinary use.
pages.media: MP4, approximately 12 seconds: begin on Actions with no filters, type System Information, select Run, hold the readable completion window for four seconds. Use a static poster of the result. No narration or music is needed; keep all written steps available below the video.

pages.title: Add your first project
pages.description: Give project-specific Actions a place to store their settings.
pages.body:
## Add a project
1. Open **Projects**.
2. Choose **Add Project** and enter a recognizable name, such as ExampleProject.
3. Select that project in the **Project** selector at the top of the window.
4. Check that the heading reads **Project Settings (for ExampleProject)**.
5. Configure the engine or platform settings needed by your next Action, or let **Configure Action** show its relevant settings when you run it.

Creating a Blackbird project does not create a game-engine project. The Blackbird project records which project you mean and the settings your installed Actions use. Select an existing engine project file or directory when asked.

## Why the fields vary
Installed Actions define many of the settings shown here. Installing another bundle can add categories or fields. Several Actions can share one setting, so entering a project file once can serve both an Open Project Action and a Build Action.

Use **Settings** for application preferences and application-scoped Action settings. Use **Projects** for the selected project's values. A setting required only for one execution can be requested immediately before that run instead.

## Bring an existing setup
Use **More > Import...** to review a Blackbird profile from another machine or teammate. Check imported paths and supply any omitted secrets before running work. Import can replace matching project entries; review the selection before accepting it.
pages.media: Two screenshots: Add Project with the synthetic name ExampleProject, then Project Settings showing that name in both the top selector and heading. Highlight those two locations together; avoid real project paths.

pages.title: Find your way around
pages.description: Understand the main window without learning every setting first.
pages.body:
## The main areas
- **Project** and **Device** at the top select the context used by applicable Actions.
- **Actions** contains individual executable tasks.
- **Workflows** contains saved sequences of queued Actions.
- **Schedules** controls when saved work runs.
- **Projects** edits the selected project's settings; **Settings** controls the app and application-scoped values.
- **History** lets you inspect earlier runs.
- **Queue** holds work prepared for later; **Output** shows messages from current activity.

You can collapse Navigation, Queue, and Output to give the main page more room. Startup visibility is configured separately in Settings. Collapsing Output does not stop an Action, and the shared progress area remains available below it. Concurrent progress bars start as one collapsed group that can be expanded.

## Navigation and views
Favorites, Recent, and pinned views narrow the Actions or Workflows you see. Their filters are separate from layout and grouping. If a list appears unexpectedly empty, clear its filters before assuming its content was removed.

Mouse Back and Forward restore previous navigation/filter views. The layout menu changes Cards/List, sorting, and grouping without changing an Action's behavior.

## Completion and support
Read the result window after a task finishes. Use Output and History for additional detail. **Send Feedback** opens the feedback flow; reviewing a report is separate from sending it. Avoid including credentials or private project content in a report.
pages.media: Annotated full-window screenshot using a public build and ExampleProject. Number the top selectors, sidebar, main page, Queue, Output, and progress area. Caption each number in text below the image; do not rely on color alone.

pages.title: Find and run Actions
pages.description: Search, filter, arrange, and run the tasks installed in Blackbird.
pages.body:
Actions perform individual tasks, such as opening a project, building an application, or collecting logs. Use the **Actions** page to find a task and run it, or add it to your queue for later.


## Try your first Action

**System Information** is a simple way to try Blackbird. It shows information about your computer without requiring a project or connected device.

1. Select **Actions** in the sidebar.
2. Select **Clear filters** if any filters are active.
3. Search for **System Information**.
4. Select **Run** on that Action.

When it finishes, a result window shows your operating system, PowerShell version, and ADB availability. You can close the window when you're done.

If ADB says **Not found**, that does not mean this Action failed. ADB is used for Android tasks; you don't need it to run System Information.


## Find the Action you need

Type in the search field to narrow the list. You can search by an Action's name or choose a suggested filter, such as a tag, **Bundle: Utilities**, or **Creator: Incogent**.

A bundle is a collection of related packages. Bundle filters are useful when you want to see the Actions installed from one collection, such as Android or Utilities.

Selected filters appear as chips below the search field:

- Select a chip's **×** to remove that filter.
- Use **Match: All** to require every selected filter.
- Use **Match: Any** to accept any selected filter.
- Select **Clear filters** to reset the search and filters.


## Choose the project and device

Before running an Action that works with a project or device, check the selectors at the top of the window.

**Project** selects the project the Action will use. For example, a build Action needs the correct project's configuration.

**Device** selects the target device. **This PC** means the computer running Blackbird. For an Action that operates on a connected device, select that device instead.

Not every Action needs both selections. Blackbird asks for required settings before starting when they haven't been configured yet. Review those settings, then continue with the run. You may also be asked for choices that apply only to this run.

## Run now or queue for later

Select **Run** to start an Action. If Blackbird asks you to review settings or confirm the operation, complete that prompt to continue.

Select **Queue** to add an Action to the queue without running it immediately. This is useful when you want to prepare several tasks before starting them.

While work is running, progress appears below **Output**. Expand Output to read the Action's messages. If several operations are running, expand the progress group to see their individual bars.

When an Action finishes, its result window reports the outcome. If it fails, follow the correction shown there. When available, **Configure Setting** takes you to the setting that needs attention. Output provides additional detail.

## Arrange the list

Open the view-options button beside the **Match** controls. Its label reflects your current layout and sorting choices.

- Choose **Cards** or **List** for the layout you prefer.
- Sort alphabetically, by recently used Actions, or by recently added Actions.
- Choose **Group: Bundle**, **Group: First tag**, or **Group: None**. Bundle grouping is the default.

Grouping changes how results are arranged. Filters determine which Actions appear.


## Can't find an Action?

Try these checks:

1. Select **Clear filters** to remove a search or filter that might hide it.
2. Open view options and check **Hide actions incompatible with selected device**. If enabled, choose a compatible device or turn the option off to see more Actions.
3. Open **Settings > Packages** and check whether the package containing the Action is installed.

If the Action appears but won't start, read the message Blackbird displays and check that the intended project and device are selected.
pages.media: Three screenshots: Actions overview with Project/Device, search and Run/Queue annotated; Bundle: Utilities chip with All/Any controls; view menu showing layout, sorting and three grouping choices. Reuse the first-Action guide video instead of producing a duplicate. Crop text at readable scale.

pages.title: Projects, settings, and shared values
pages.description: Understand where settings come from and why Actions can share them.
pages.body:
## Actions introduce settings
An Action declares the information it needs. Blackbird turns those declarations into settings controls, validates the entered values, and supplies the values when that Action runs. You do not need to edit JSON to configure an Action.

Some settings are deliberately shared. For example, Open Godot Project and Export Godot Build both use the same Godot project setting. Change that project's value once and subsequent runs of both Actions receive it.

## Choose the right scope
| Scope | Where you edit it | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Project | Projects, or Configure Action | A separate value for each selected project |
| Application | Settings > Action Settings, or Configure Action | A value shared across this Blackbird installation |
| Run | The run or queue configuration prompt | A choice for that execution |

Remembered run values are suggestions for a future prompt, not a replacement for persistent project settings. Secret run values are not remembered.

## Configure an Action
1. Select the intended project and device.
2. Open the Action's menu and choose **Configure Action**, or follow the configuration prompt shown when a required setting is missing.
3. Fill in the visible required fields. Some fields appear only after another selection makes them applicable.
4. Save and run the Action. Review any run-specific choices before continuing.

Named options give one setting several named alternatives. Profiles select a group of related settings together, such as a build target and output directory. One available option/profile can resolve automatically; multiple alternatives require a choice.

## What is shared, and what is not
Sharing is based on the setting's exact identity, not two controls having the same label. An Action-specific setting stays with that Action. A profile is owned by its Action and project; it is not a global variable store.

Queued items retain captured configuration. Changing a project setting does not silently rewrite values already saved into a queue item or Workflow. Edit and review that saved item when you intend to update it. Authors can learn the underlying identities in [Sharing settings](../../authoring/shared-settings/).
pages.media: Diagram: two Action cards point to a single Project Settings field and each receives its value on a new run. Below it, show an already queued item retaining its earlier value. Screenshot: Configure Action with project, application and run-scope concepts annotated using synthetic fields.

pages.title: Select and refresh devices
pages.description: Choose the target for device-aware Actions.
pages.body:
## Select a target
**This PC** is the computer running Blackbird. It is always available and is not a SteamOS device. Use the Device selector to choose a verified connected target for Actions that require one.

1. Connect and prepare your device using its platform's setup guide.
2. Select the refresh button beside **Device**.
3. Wait for the scan's progress to finish.
4. Select the intended device and check its name before running a deployment or cleanup.

Discovery can also run at startup when **Discover Devices on Startup** is enabled. It does not continuously poll for changes. Scan warnings appear in Output; refresh after changing a connection or authorization.

## Compatibility and separate endpoints
An Action may require a particular device kind. The view option **Hide actions incompatible with selected device** can hide unavailable Actions. Showing an Action does not make an incompatible target usable.

A Steam Frame host and its Android/Lepton endpoint are separate targets. Select the Android endpoint for Android Actions and the SteamOS host for supported SteamOS Actions. Do not assume all Actions are enabled for every SteamOS device simply because SSH is available.

## Queued targets
An item using **Current device** resolves the selected device when that item starts. A pinned device stays fixed even when the top selector changes. The command-line or schedule override only replaces Current device; it does not replace an explicitly pinned target.

An unavailable or unverified target causes a reported error. Blackbird does not silently deploy to another device instead.
pages.media: Screenshot: Device selector with This PC and synthetic verified device names. Second image: a queue item showing Current device beside a separate example pinned to a specific target. Explain that a Frame host and Android endpoint are distinct entries.

pages.title: Prepare and run a queue
pages.description: Arrange several Actions and review their saved settings before execution.
pages.body:
## Prepare the work
1. Find an Action and select **Queue**.
2. Complete any requested configuration. Repeat for the other tasks you want to run.
3. Open the Queue panel and arrange items in their intended order.
4. Edit an item to review its project, parameter values, profile, and device target. Remove items you no longer need.
5. Select the queue's Run control when the sequence is ready.

A useful sequence might build a project, deploy its output, and launch it. Each Action must be configured correctly; placing Actions together does not automatically pass arbitrary script variables between them. Use shared settings or explicit files when tasks need the same information.

## Saved settings and device choice
Queue items capture resolved configuration. Later changes to package defaults or a project's profile do not silently replace that saved configuration. After changing a setting, edit the item if you want it to use the new value.

**Current device** is different: it is resolved when the item begins. Pin a target in the item editor when it must use one specific device. A library or parameter change that makes a saved item invalid requires review before execution.

## Pause, stop, and inspect
**Pause after current action** lets the running Action finish before the queue pauses. Stop requests cancellation of active work; it does not undo completed file changes, installs, or uploads. Review results before restarting a partially completed sequence.

Follow progress below Output, and use the completion result and History to inspect what ran. If a task fails, address the reported cause and review remaining work rather than assuming the sequence completed.

## Reuse the sequence
Save the queue as a Workflow when you want to load or schedule it again. A Workflow is a saved sequence, while the visible queue is your current working copy.
pages.media: MP4, 15–20 seconds: queue two safe System Information examples, edit one, reorder them, then start. Hold the order and item detail long enough to read. Separate screenshot: Pause after current action control with a caption distinguishing it from Stop.

pages.title: Save and reuse Workflows
pages.description: Turn a configured queue into a reusable sequence.
pages.body:
## Save a Workflow
1. Prepare and review the Actions in your queue.
2. Use the queue's save command and give the Workflow a meaningful name.
3. Open **Workflows** to find the saved sequence.
4. Use its load/edit controls to review or revise it, then save the intended changes.

Saved Workflows keep their Action configurations. They are useful for repeatable tasks such as building and deploying a particular project. Search, tags, favorites, and views help you find them as the collection grows.

## Load versus run
Loading makes a Workflow available in the queue for review. Manually running a Workflow loads its sequence into the visible queue and starts it. Review or save unsaved queue work before replacing it with another Workflow.

Scheduled Workflows behave differently: they run a separate execution copy and do not replace the visible queue. Use the schedule monitor and History to follow that work.

## Maintain a Workflow
After editing an Action's settings or updating a package, review the Workflow's captured values. Blackbird validates them against the installed Action's current requirements. A removed Action or incompatible saved value must be corrected; it is not silently substituted with a different Action or a new default.

If a Workflow uses Current device, its items can follow the current selection or a schedule/CLI override. Pin individual items when the sequence intentionally uses different devices.
pages.media: Screenshots: saving a synthetic Verify Project Workflow, its Workflows entry, and its loaded queue. Annotate Load and Run as different outcomes. No upload or destructive Actions in the demonstration.

pages.title: Schedule Actions and Workflows
pages.description: Set a time for saved work and inspect the result.
pages.body:
## Create a schedule
1. Run the Action or Workflow manually first and resolve missing tools, settings, and credentials.
2. Save the Workflow if scheduling a sequence.
3. Open **Schedules** and choose **New Schedule**.
4. Name it, select its target, and choose a one-time, daily, or selected-weekday time.
5. Review the device override, enabled state, and available wake/missed-start options, then save.
6. Use **Run Now** to check the configured target without waiting for the timer.

Run Now and timer-triggered work use a separate execution copy. They do not replace your visible queue or unsaved edits. A running indicator opens the monitor; results appear in History.

## Timing and overlapping work
Windows Task Scheduler provides the launch timing. Wake behavior depends on the computer's firmware and Windows power policy. Missed-start options do not guarantee execution while the required interactive user is unavailable.

Scheduled work is serialized. If another run occupies the execution slot, later requests wait and report their queued state rather than running simultaneously. Consider build duration when choosing start times.

## Keep scheduled work usable
Ensure devices remain reachable and required authentication is available. A workflow that asks for interactive input is not automatically an unattended workflow. Review it before relying on an overnight run.

Use the calendar and schedule editor to review, disable, reschedule, or delete a definition. Inspect a failed occurrence in History. If task synchronization reports an issue, use Blackbird's schedule synchronization controls instead of deleting configuration files.
pages.media: Three screenshots: New Schedule with a synthetic daily verification job; calendar with enabled/disabled entries; History showing a completed and queued scheduled run. MP4 optional: edit a schedule and use Run Now, without waiting for a clock transition.

pages.title: Results, Output, and History
pages.description: Understand what happened and collect the right diagnostics.
pages.body:
## Read the completion window
An Action's completion window reports success or failure and any available next step. A known configuration failure can offer **Configure Setting**, which opens and highlights the field needing attention. An **Open Folder** or copy control may be available when the Action returns files or values.

Output is supporting detail, not the only indication that something failed. Expand it to inspect messages while work runs. Background operations identify themselves there even if their progress bar was visible only briefly.

## Inspect a past run
1. Open **History**.
2. Locate the run by its Action, time, or available filters.
3. Open its details and inspect the result and log.
4. If using **Run Again**, review the intended project, device, and whether repeating the operation is safe. Repeating an upload or cleanup has real effects.

Where a saved configuration is available, Run Again uses that captured run configuration. Older entries may require the normal configuration flow. A history entry records a run; it does not restore a previous filesystem state.

## Share a useful report
Record the Action name, app/package version, time, expected outcome, and exact error. Include the relevant log rather than an unrelated full desktop screenshot. Review attachments for secrets, personal paths, and proprietary data. **Report Issue** or **Send Feedback** lets you review the report before sending it.

If a log has been removed, explain that in the report. Do not rerun a destructive or externally visible task just to recreate a screenshot unless you intend its effects.
pages.media: Screenshot: understood failure with Configure Setting and a second screenshot of History details. Use a synthetic missing-folder error and a short sample log with no credentials. Annotate result summary versus diagnostic detail.

pages.title: Set up Android tools and devices
pages.description: Prepare ADB and verify a connected Android target.
pages.body:
## Install the tools
Get Android SDK Platform-Tools from the [Android developer site](https://developer.android.com/tools/releases/platform-tools). Extract the complete distribution rather than copying only adb.exe. Configure Blackbird's ADB path in Settings to use that executable when automatic discovery cannot find it.

Some build/deployment Actions also require **Android AAPT2 executable** to inspect APK metadata. AAPT2 comes from Android SDK Build-Tools, not Platform-Tools. Configure its path when the Action requests it.

## Connect and authorize
1. Enable the device's developer/debugging access using its manufacturer's instructions.
2. Connect with a data-capable USB cable, or establish its supported network ADB connection.
3. Accept the device's debugging authorization prompt for your computer.
4. Refresh devices in Blackbird and choose the verified Android target.
5. Run **List Android Devices** if you need additional connection detail.

If no device appears, check cable/driver support and authorization before changing project settings. An offline or unauthorized ADB endpoint is not ready for deployment.

## Configure the project
Set **Android package ID** to your application's package identity. Set **Android build directory** to the directory containing the build you intend to deploy. These are project facts shared by compatible Android Actions, not the identity of the physical device.

Use [Deploy and launch on Android](../../tasks/android/) after discovery succeeds. For a Steam Frame running Lepton, select its Android endpoint for Android Actions; native SteamOS access is a separate connection.
pages.media: Screenshots: ADB path setting pointing to C:\Tools\Android\platform-tools\adb.exe; device selector with a synthetic Android device. Device-side authorization screenshot should obscure the host fingerprint and personal device identity.

pages.title: Set up a SteamOS device
pages.description: Pair a development host and verify SteamOS discovery.
pages.body:
## Prepare and pair the device
Follow Valve's [development-device setup and pairing instructions](https://partner.steamgames.com/doc/steamdeck/loadgames) for your supported device. Complete pairing with this development computer before expecting Blackbird's SSH-based operations to work. Keep the device and computer on a network that permits the connection.

Blackbird uses the paired development-host key and verifies the connection. Running the Devkit Client GUI is not required for every later operation once pairing is available. A host answering on the network is not sufficient evidence that authentication succeeded.

## Discover it in Blackbird
1. Enable the relevant development service on the device.
2. Refresh the Device selector in Blackbird.
3. Select the verified SteamOS target.
4. Check Output for scan warnings if it does not appear.

If local host-name discovery fails, review the configured SteamOS host list in Settings and use the correct reachable host address. Do not use an Android serial in place of a SteamOS host.

## Choose the right target and build
Steam Deck, Steam Machine, and Steam Frame retain their supported device kinds in the current app. Actions decide which kinds they support. A Frame's Lepton Android endpoint is separate from its native SteamOS target; Lepton does not need to be running to verify the native connection.

Configure the build profile and runtime for the artifact you are installing. A Windows, Linux, or Android build needs an appropriate runtime and target; successful file transfer alone does not prove it can launch.
pages.media: Screenshot: verified synthetic SteamOS device beside a separate Android endpoint. Caption which Actions use each. Second screenshot: discovery warning with a synthetic unreachable hostname, showing where to find the warning without exposing SSH keys.

pages.title: Configure Unreal Engine
pages.description: Point Blackbird at the engine installation and existing Unreal project.
pages.body:
## Prerequisites
Install the Unreal Engine version required by the project and the platform toolchain needed for your target. Confirm the project opens in that engine before automating it. Use [Epic's packaging documentation](https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/packaging-your-project) for engine/platform requirements.

## Set the paths
1. Install the Unreal bundle under **Settings > Packages**.
2. Select your Blackbird project and open its Unreal settings, or configure **Open UE Project**.
3. Set **Unreal project** to its .uproject file.
4. Set **Unreal Engine installation** to the installation folder containing the Engine directory, not to RunUAT.bat itself.
5. Run the open-project Action to check the association.

Build profiles can additionally select a **Build target** .Target.cs file. Blackbird derives the target name from that file. Keep engine/project paths project-specific when projects use different engine versions.

## Before packaging
Configure the engine's own maps, plugins, signing, SDKs, and target-platform settings. Blackbird passes the selected build configuration to the engine; it does not make an incompatible project or missing SDK usable.

For Android, **Target platform** and **Android cook flavor** are separate selections. Use a flavor supported by your engine/project. If a tool path or prerequisite fails, correct that reported setting and retry the small validation/open step before a long build.
pages.media: Screenshot: Unreal settings with synthetic engine installation and .uproject paths. Annotate the Engine-containing directory versus project file. A packaging profile screenshot belongs in the build guide, not duplicated here.

pages.title: Configure Unity
pages.description: Select the project and matching Unity Editor.
pages.body:
## Prepare the project
Install the required Unity Editor and platform modules through Unity Hub or your supported installation process. Open the project in Unity first and resolve licensing or package-import issues. See [Unity Hub documentation](https://docs.unity3d.com/hub/manual/index.html) for installing editors and modules.

## Configure Blackbird
1. Install the Unity bundle.
2. Select the Blackbird project and set **Unity project** to the root containing Assets, Packages, and ProjectSettings.
3. Set **Unity editor installation** to the installation folder containing the Editor directory when you need to choose explicitly.
4. Otherwise configure **Unity Hub** and allow Blackbird to locate the exact version recorded by the project.
5. Use **Open Unity Project** to verify the paths.

Blackbird does not silently replace a missing pinned editor with the newest installed editor. Install the required version or deliberately update the project in Unity.

## Choose a build backend
The Build Unity Project Action supports **Automatic**, **Unity 6 native build**, **Blackbird managed build**, and **Custom static editor method**. Which is appropriate depends on the installed editor and project. Do not select Unity 6-specific capabilities for an older editor.

A custom editor method must already exist in the project and implement its build behavior. Blackbird is not a replacement for writing or validating that method. Continue with the Unity build guide once the project opens successfully.
pages.media: Screenshot: Unity project root and matching editor installation settings. Show a synthetic project pinned to an installed editor without suggesting that all Unity versions use the same native build-profile options.

pages.title: Configure Godot
pages.description: Choose the editor, project, and export prerequisites.
pages.body:
## Prepare Godot
Install the editor required by the project. Open the project in Godot and check that it loads. For exporting, install matching export templates and create a preset in Godot's Export window. Follow the [Godot export guide](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/tutorials/export/exporting_projects.html) for platform-specific requirements.

## Configure Blackbird
1. Install the Godot bundle.
2. Select your Blackbird project.
3. Set **Godot project** to project.godot.
4. Set **Godot editor executable** to the editor you intend to use.
5. Run **Open Godot Project** and verify the intended project opens.

Open and export Actions reuse these compatible Godot settings. You do not need a separate copy of the project path for each Action.

## Prepare export
Create and test the export preset inside Godot. Its name must match the **Export preset** selected in Blackbird. Choose an output file appropriate for the preset and export mode.

If export reports missing templates, install templates matching the configured editor. If it cannot find the preset, check the selected project and saved preset name rather than changing the editor executable blindly. Platform signing and SDK requirements still apply when the export is launched through Blackbird.
pages.media: Two screenshots: Godot path settings and a synthetic export preset name shown in both Godot and Blackbird. Do not capture signing credentials or private export configuration.

pages.title: Package an Unreal project
pages.description: Configure and run Package UE Build and check its output.
pages.body:
## Before running
Install the relevant package bundle and complete its tool/device setup. Confirm the task manually on a small or disposable build before adding it to an unattended sequence.

## Steps
1. Select the intended project and configure the Unreal engine/project paths.
2. Configure a build profile with Build target, Target platform, Client configuration, and Archive directory.
3. For Android, choose the applicable cook flavor; review build, staging, packaging, and prerequisite options.
4. Run Package UE Build and review the selected profile before confirming.
5. Inspect the completion result and packaged files in the configured archive directory.

## If it fails
Choose output and cleanup options deliberately. Cleaning generated staging/build output can remove earlier results. Additional arguments are an advanced escape hatch, not a substitute for a correct engine/project configuration. On failure, inspect the first meaningful UAT error and the recorded log; do not assume the final process-exit line identifies the underlying cause.

## Repeat the task
Save useful configuration as a named profile where offered, then queue the Action or save a Workflow. Review captured settings when changing target platforms or output paths.
pages.media: Screenshot: the Package UE Build configuration with a synthetic ExampleProject profile; annotate only the fields required for the steps above. Second screenshot: its completion result and output location with personal paths removed. Optional MP4: choose the profile, start, then cut to the result with an explicit “build/transfer time omitted” caption; never imply the operation is instantaneous.

pages.title: Build a Unity project
pages.description: Configure and run Build Unity Project and check its output.
pages.body:
## Before running
Install the relevant package bundle and complete its tool/device setup. Confirm the task manually on a small or disposable build before adding it to an unattended sequence.

## Steps
1. Select the project and verify its exact editor installation.
2. Configure a build profile: backend, Build target, Build output, and Output file name as applicable.
3. For a native Unity 6 build, select the Unity 6 build profile asset. For a custom backend, supply its static editor method.
4. Review optional API updates, graphics mode, and additional arguments before running.
5. Run Build Unity Project and inspect the result and files at the selected output.

## If it fails
The selected backend controls which fields apply. A custom editor method must return a meaningful failure when its build fails; a method that exits successfully without producing the expected artifact needs correction in the project. Licensing, editor imports, and missing platform modules remain Unity prerequisites.

## Repeat the task
Save useful configuration as a named profile where offered, then queue the Action or save a Workflow. Review captured settings when changing target platforms or output paths.

## Choose the source
Use the installed log Action for the system that failed, such as **Pull Android App Logs**, **Record Android Device Logs**, or **Pull Steam Logs**. Existing app logs and a live device recording answer different questions: a recording captures events while you reproduce the issue.

## Collect
1. Select the correct project and verified device when the Action needs them.

3. Run the log Action and follow its recording/stop instructions if it is a live capture.
4. Reproduce the problem while recording, if applicable.

pages.title: Update a project version
pages.description: Choose each version component and optionally include a VCS revision.
pages.body:
## Configure the format
In Project Settings, configure **Version format** as an ordered list. Available sources include Major, Minor, Patch, Build counter, Calendar date, and Version control revision. A source can appear once. Components are joined with periods; these custom formats are not necessarily Semantic Versioning.

Examples include Major.Minor.Patch and Major.Minor.Patch.Version control revision. Android numeric build codes remain separate. Ensure your distribution platform accepts the resulting format.

## Run the update
1. Select the project and engine for Update Project Version.
2. Review the ordered format and Calendar date format if used.
3. Choose the counter operation, such as incrementing a named counter or Last counter. Reset following counters affects counters to its right, not date/revision components.
4. Use **Refresh generated components** to refresh date/revision without incrementing counters, or **Set explicitly** to seed a complete version in the configured order.
5. Run and inspect the reported old/new value and engine files.

After reordering components, use Set explicitly to establish the intended counter positions. Old version-scheme settings are not converted automatically; update saved Workflows and queued items that use them.

## Version control
Install Version Control support when available and configure the project's VCS. Git uses local HEAD (an abbreviated hexadecimal commit ID), Perforce uses the highest submitted changelist represented by synced files under the folder, and Unity Version Control uses the loaded changeset of a full workspace. Configure and authenticate the installed git, p4, or cm client separately. Blackbird does not provide checkout, sync, or commit operations.

Git does not require a particular hosting service or remote. Local changes and linked repositories are not fully described by one revision ID. Perforce's number does not prove a consistent workspace snapshot; partial UVCS workspaces without one loaded changeset are rejected. A failed revision lookup stops the version change.

## Prepare a publishing profile
Upload Build supports Steam, Meta Quest/Rift, PICO, STOVE, Viveport PC, and Custom CLI. It uses separately installed vendor tools and your authorized account. Having an Action installed does not grant access to a storefront application.

1. Build and inspect the artifact you intend to upload.
2. Select the project and configure **Upload Build**.
3. Create or select a publishing profile and choose its **Uploader**.
4. Fill in the provider-specific tool path, application identity, artifact location, destination, and credentials. Follow the matching provider guide.
5. Run with **Validate without uploading** enabled. Resolve every local configuration problem it reports.
6. Review the profile and destination again, then run with validation-only disabled when you intend to upload.

Validation checks configuration and preparation; it does not prove that the remote service will accept your credentials, account permissions, build, or publishing policy. Keep provider-specific preview modes distinct from Blackbird's validation-only switch.

## Confirm the outcome
Read the completion result and inspect the destination in the provider dashboard. An upload is not necessarily a public release. Conversely, a live-branch option can have immediate effects; review it before confirming.

For a failed transfer, inspect the meaningful provider error, not just its process exit code. Check authentication, the chosen app, and the build's platform/identity. Do not repeatedly rerun uploads without checking whether the previous attempt created a remote build.

pages.description: Connect a command-line uploader with explicit arguments and result rules.
pages.body:
## Prepare the command
Use this adapter when a supported command-line program can upload your artifact but has no dedicated Blackbird provider. Obtain it from its vendor, authenticate through its supported process, and first understand its command-line contract. Blackbird cannot infer the correct flags or upload policy for an arbitrary tool.

## Configure the profile
1. Select **Custom CLI** as the Uploader.
2. Choose **CLI tool** and **Working directory**.
3. Set **Build or upload descriptor**, **Application ID**, and **Channel** when your tool uses them.
4. Add each argument using the argument editor. Keep a path with spaces as one argument; do not construct an extra shell command string to work around quoting.
5. Configure environment variables needed by the tool and use the available secret handling for credentials.
6. Set **Success exit codes** and, if needed, **Required success output** and **Failure output** patterns according to the tool's documented behavior.
7. Run **Validate without uploading**, then test a real upload to a non-production destination.

## Be precise about success
A process returning zero is not always proof that the intended remote operation happened. Conversely, informational text on standard error is not necessarily a failure. Configure the contract to match the tool, then verify the remote artifact manually during setup.

Validation-only checks Blackbird's local preparation; it is not a universal vendor dry-run switch. If the vendor offers a dry-run argument, deliberately configure and review it. Avoid patterns so broad that an unrelated message can be interpreted as success.

## Diagnose a failure
Use the same executable version and working directory when reproducing a command outside Blackbird. Check argument boundaries, missing environment values, expiration of authentication, and output patterns. Never paste a credential-bearing command into feedback or public chat.

pages.title: Install, update, and remove packages
pages.description: Choose the Actions and support packages available in your library.
pages.body:
## Understand bundles and packages
A package is an Action, shared library, or discovery provider. A bundle groups related packages. Actions appear on the Actions page; libraries support scripts and providers find devices, so they do not appear as runnable Action cards.

## Review a change
1. Open **Settings > Packages**.
2. Use **Check for Updates** to discover available releases.
3. Expand a bundle to inspect its packages. Review installed/available versions and **Release Notes**.
4. Select the bundle or individual packages you want. Clearing an installed selection proposes removal.
5. Read the Install/Update/Remove summary and choose **Apply Changes**.
6. Confirm the summarized change, follow progress, and read the completion window.

**Discard Changes** abandons the pending selection. Dependency validation can require support libraries for Actions you retain. System Information is required for the tutorial and cannot be removed through ordinary selection.

## Undo and failure
**Undo Last Update** restores the supported previous package state. It is one rollback opportunity, not unlimited version history or a backup of every custom edit. Review its result; not every local/official ownership change can be undone automatically.

If a change fails, read its completion error and Output. Close a program specifically identified as using affected files, then retry. Do not delete the library or alter internal metadata to force removal. Installed package files may be preserved when activation fails.

## Customize separately
Keep published package content intact. Use the available duplicate/fork or new-Action authoring flow for editable local work. Updates and local customization are different operations; changing a signed file directly can prevent it from validating.

Use a disposable example selection and show System Information retained. Separate Undo screenshot should explain the single rollback rather than imply arbitrary historical versions.

pages.title: Choose or move the package library
pages.description: Keep installed packages and local content in the intended folder.
pages.body:
## Find the active location
Open **Settings > Packages** and read **Package library location**. The library contains installed bundles and project configuration. Logs and temporary/cache data are stored separately; moving the library does not mean every Blackbird file moves with it.

## Change Location versus Move Library
**Change Location...** selects the library to use after restart. It does not copy your current library into that folder. Use it to switch to a different library intentionally.

**Move Library** relocates the current library. Choose a writable, empty destination separate from the source, and review the confirmation. Do not select a parent/child folder or expect two existing libraries to merge. Let active work finish and close external editors or applications using files there before moving.

## Local package folders
Custom packages created through the app are stored in My Actions. The layout is `Bundles/user.actions/<package-id>/`, with the package manifest and script together. Use the Action editor for manifest changes; edit its script in your preferred editor and reload Actions afterward.

Official and local bundles each have their own folder beneath Bundles. Internal configuration files are managed by Blackbird. A directory being visible does not mean it is safe to rename or remove while the app or an Action is using it.

## Backups and old Actions
Use reviewed profile exports for portable configuration and custom Actions. Keep a separate backup before reorganizing files. Old flat Packages content is not automatically executable in the new bundle library; import custom Actions through the supported flow instead of copying official packages into My Actions.

pages.body:
## Export
1. Open **More > Export...**.
2. Choose **Current Project**, **Everything**, or adjust selections to create a Custom export.
3. Review included projects, Workflows, Actions, settings, and machine-specific paths.
4. Leave secrets excluded unless you explicitly need a protected transfer and understand the contents.
5. Save the .bbprofile file and keep it in an appropriate location.

Current Project is useful for sharing one project setup; Everything is a broad configuration transfer. Neither is a copy of your game project's source files or build artifacts. License/trial state, logs, history, and transient discovered devices are not exported. Packages marked non-exportable are excluded.

## Import
1. Back up the configuration you may replace.
2. Open **More > Import...** and select a .bbprofile or supported standalone .blackbird-action.zip.
3. Review the proposed contents and matching items.
4. Confirm the intended import.
5. Review local tool/project paths and supply omitted credentials, then test a safe Action.

Import is additive for unrelated content, but included matching projects/Workflows and Action IDs can replace existing entries. A section absent from the file is not an instruction to erase your setup. A profile requiring a newer Blackbird version must be opened with a compatible app.

## Treat imported scripts as code
Only import Actions from a source you trust and inspect their scripts before execution. A friendly label or creator field is not proof of safety. Do not send a profile containing secrets or private machine paths to a public issue tracker.

pages.title: Create your first custom Action
pages.description: Build a complete, read-only Action and understand each file.
pages.body:
## What you will make
Create **Report Output Directory**, which reads a project setting and reports its value. It does not modify that directory. You will use the same setting in a second Action later.

An Action package contains a **package.json** manifest describing its identity, requirements, settings, and entrypoint, plus a **run.ps1** script containing its behavior. Blackbird's editor writes the manifest; the runtime supplies the configured values to the script.

## Create it in the app
1. Select **New Action** and name it Report Output Directory. Use the ID `report-output-directory` and a relevant tag such as Utilities.
2. Add a custom setting with shared namespace `example`, key `outputDirectory`, label **Output directory**, type **Folder**, scope **Project**, and Required enabled.
3. Enable **Requires an active project**. This example needs no device and is not destructive.
4. On **Execution**, choose the Windows PowerShell file-based starter. Keep its runtime import and unhandled-failure trap.
5. Create the Action, open its package folder through the Action's menu, and edit run.ps1 as below.
6. Reload Actions, select a test project, and configure Output directory to an existing disposable folder.
7. Run the Action. Its completion window should report the same path you configured.

```powershell
Import-Module (Join-Path $env:BLACKBIRD_RUNTIME_ROOT 'Blackbird.Runtime.psm1') -Force
trap { Set-BlackbirdUnhandledFailureResult -ErrorRecord $_; break }

$OutputDirectory = Get-BlackbirdParameter -Name 'example.outputDirectory' -Required
if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $OutputDirectory -PathType Container)) {
    Set-BlackbirdFailureResult -Title 'Folder unavailable' -Message 'The configured output directory is unavailable.' -Guidance 'Choose an existing Output directory for this project and run again.'
    throw 'Output directory is unavailable.'
}
Write-Output 'Read the configured output directory.'
Set-BlackbirdSuccessResult -Title 'Output directory' -Message 'The project setting was read successfully.' -Items @($OutputDirectory)
```

## Why it works
`example.outputDirectory` is Blackbird's setting identity. `$OutputDirectory` is an ordinary variable inside this PowerShell run. The helper reads the already resolved setting; assigning to the PowerShell variable would not change Blackbird's saved value.

Start it from Blackbird, not by double-clicking run.ps1. Blackbird supplies the invocation context and result channel. An error saying BLACKBIRD_CONTEXT_PATH is missing means that required launch context was not provided.

## Files and examples
The app saves custom packages under `Bundles/user.actions/<package-id>/` in your chosen library. Use Edit Action for manifest changes and your editor for script changes. The [complete example ZIP](/assets/blackbird/docs/examples/shared-settings.zip) contains this Action and the second read-only Action. Inspect the files, then copy their individual package folders into My Actions in a test library and reload; this ZIP is a source example, not an Import-format archive.

pages.body:
## The value journey
**An Action declares an input → Blackbird shows a control → the user supplies a value → Blackbird resolves it for the run → the script reads it.**

The declaration is a definition, not the current value. For a project-scoped setting, two projects can have different values under the same identity. The Action package does not need to be rewritten when a user changes that value.

| Concept | Example | How a PowerShell script reads it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Action parameter | `example.outputDirectory` | `Get-BlackbirdParameter -Name 'example.outputDirectory'` |
| Generic Blackbird variable | `BuildFlavor` | `Get-BlackbirdVariable -Name 'BuildFlavor'` |
| Selected project/device | Current execution context | `Get-BlackbirdProject` / `Get-BlackbirdDevice` |
| Local script variable | `$OutputDirectory` | Ordinary PowerShell syntax |
| Environment variable | `$env:BLACKBIRD_PACKAGE_ROOT` | Environment supplied to the process |

## Prefer declared settings for new Action inputs
Parameters have labels, types, required-state validation, and project/application/run scope. Define them in **New/Edit Action > Custom Settings**. They are the normal way to give users an editable input such as a project path or tool choice.

Generic variables are a separate string dictionary in the invocation context. Project variables override same-named global variables there. They do not automatically become typed Action settings, and a parameter and variable with similar names are not interchangeable. If adapting an older script using a generic variable, identify its actual source rather than assuming a Custom Setting populates it.

## Scope is separate from namespace
The namespace groups and identifies a setting; scope determines which value is used. `example.outputDirectory` can be a shared project setting, while `example.toolPath` could be an application setting. A namespace named after a tool does not automatically mean application scope.

**This Action** uses the package ID as its namespace. A shared namespace is deliberately reusable. Profiles group multiple related project settings into presets; they do not create a new global scope.

## No automatic output handoff
Actions run in separate processes. A local variable in Action A is not visible in Action B. Reading a shared setting does not write it. To exchange produced data, use an explicit artifact or supported external system and configure both Actions to refer to it. Do not modify Blackbird configuration files from scripts.
